ImageDescription.value: The rock pigeon, scientifically known as **Columba livia**, is a familiar bird commonly found in urban areas, rural regions, and hilly terrains. Their primary habitats include vacant spaces in buildings, caves, and open rocky areas. In terms of diet, they primarily feed on grains, seeds, and occasionally small fruits. Their gray-colored body, black wings, and neck with a greenish or purplish sheen are distinctive features. They possess remarkable navigational abilities and have historical significance as domesticated pigeons. This photograph was taken in Salt Lake, Kolkata, on April 3, 2025.

145434219.title: File:Lake Michigan and the United States (MODIS 2018-10-25).jpg

ImageDescription.value:
On October 21, 2018, the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) acquired a true-color image of the southern shore of Lake Michigan and surrounding countryside.

The deep blue waters of Lake Michigan are colored in pale blues, tans, and green along the southern shoreline. A small part of the coloration may be due to algae or phytoplankton—microscopic plant-like organisms that live in these waters and can grow remarkably when conditions are right—but the primary cause of this color appears to be from sediment stirred from the light-colored bottom of the lake.

Sediment most often colors Lake Michigan in the spring and the fall when transitioning weather patterns bring storms and strong winds. The winds stir the water, pulling quartz sand and silt from the lake bottom to the surface. White sand looks milky blue when viewed through the water from space. The southern shore of Lake Michigan is rimmed with sandy beaches, such as Indiana Dunes State Park where sand dunes rise to almost 200 feet along a series of ridges and valleys. These dunes are a result of glacial movement and retreat, and are also a source of sediment movement along the shoreline.

The tan lands to the south of Lake Michigan are prairie lands, much of which have been recruited for agriculture. As autumn progresses, prairie grasses and crops such as corn and soybean turn tan in color. Irregular green streaks within the prairies mark the banks of rivers and streams, where trees and bushes grow. Further south the prairie gives way to more rolling, hilly land where forests and shrublands remain green.

While much of Illinois and Indiana are rich in agricultural, several large cities are also found in the region. Cities appear as gray pixels in true-color images. The large city of Chicago, Illinois, along with neighboring cities such as Naperville, Illinois and Gary, Indiana are marked by gray pixels on the southwestern tip of Lake Michigan. To the southeast, Indianapolis, Indiana can be seen sitting close to the transition between grassland and hillier green topography. A smudge of gray pixels south of Indianapolis is Louisville, Kentucky, which is located in rolling green hills.

Artist.value: MODIS Land Rapid Response Team, NASA GSFC

The Gardens of Villa Melzi strech out along the lake shore and are harmoniously inserted into the hilly scenery of the Bellagio peninsula that divides the two branches of the

lake. Inland, the Villa, the Chapel and the orangery, today transformed into a historical museum, are splendid expression of neo-classical style and as such stated national monument. This architectural complex was realized between 1808 and 1810 for Francesco Melzi d'Eril (1753-1816), Duke of Lodi, Vice President of Italian Republic under Napoleon and afterwards Gran Chancellor of the Napoleonic Reign of Italy. Francesco Melzi d'Eril relied upon the architect and decorator Giocondo Albertolli (1742-1839), an exponent of great importance in neo-classicism, asking for a villa looking sober and polished whose simples lines and volumes would emphasise the surrounding amazing countryside. The Villa that became the Melzi's residence at the end of his political career and afterwards his summer residence until his death was decorated and furnished by some of the most famous artists of the age: as well as along with Giocondo Albertolli author of the great part of furniture and inside decorations, are to be noted the painters Andrea Appiani (1754-1817) and Giuseppe Bossi (1777-1815), Alessandro Sanquirico (1777-1849) and the sculptors Antonio Canova (1757-1822), Giambattista Comolli (1775-1830), Pompeo Marchesi (1789-1858), as well as the bronze sculptor Luigi Manfredini (1771-1840). The English styled gardens, enriched with sculptures, was designed by the architect Luigi Canonica and by the botanist Luigi Villoresi, both responsible for the arrangement of Villa Reale park in Monza. Through the contribution of great artists and artisans and the special concordance between them and Francesco Melzi the whole complex was shaped like a place of rare harmony and was admired, among the others, by Stendhal who described its beauty in his book "Rome, Naples, Florence" dated 1817.
